Start with the need, not the money

The most common mistake is to look for "funding" first and decide what to do with it later. Funders and lenders spot this at once. Start instead with one **specific need** that you can describe in a single sentence: what you will buy or do, what it costs, and what result it will produce in numbers.
Weak: "I need money to grow my fashion business."

Strong: "I need one industrial straight-stitch machine and one overlock machine, about ₦650,000 (approximate) together, so I can sew 40 school uniforms a week instead of 15 and accept the two school contracts I turned down last term."

The strong version tells anyone reading it what the money buys, why, and how it will pay for itself. It also tells **you** which type of funding fits. A machine that lets you accept paid orders you are already being offered can be repaid from those orders, so a loan or a supplier partnership is reasonable. A training programme for ten unemployed young women in your area does not repay itself directly, so a grant is the natural fit.

If the need earns money back quickly and reliably, borrowing can work; if it does not, look to grants, partners or your own savings.
Three questions that decide the route

**Will this need bring money back?** New stock, a machine for orders you already have, or packaging that lets you enter a supermarket usually will. A website redesign or a fancy signboard may not, at least not in a way you can measure.

**How soon, and how much?** Write the extra profit per month that the need will produce, and how many months until it starts. A loan repayment usually starts within a month of disbursement, so a slow return is a danger sign for borrowing.

**Can someone else supply the thing instead of the money?** A supplier who gives you 30 days to pay, a buyer who pays a deposit upfront, or a cooperative that shares a machine can remove the need for cash entirely.
Worked example: one need, three possible routes

For example, Hauwa runs a tailoring shop in Kaduna. A secondary school has offered her an order for 300 uniforms at ₦9,000 each (approximate), paid in two halves: 50% on order and 50% on delivery. Fabric and trims cost about ₦4,200 per uniform. She needs a second machine, about ₦350,000 (approximate), to deliver in eight weeks.
The 50% deposit is ₦1,350,000. That covers all the materials (₦1,260,000) with ₦90,000 left over.
The machine is the real gap: ₦350,000 minus the ₦90,000 left from the deposit = ₦260,000 still needed.
Route A, own money: she has ₦150,000 saved, but it is her only buffer. Using all of it leaves no safety.
Route B, partnership: she asks the machine dealer about paying in instalments over three months. The dealer agrees to ₦120,000 down and ₦80,000 a month for three months, a total of ₦360,000.
Route C, loan: a microfinance bank quotes a loan that would cost more in interest and fees than the dealer's ₦10,000 extra, and takes two to three weeks to approve.

Hauwa pays the dealer's ₦120,000 deposit from savings, keeps ₦30,000 as a buffer, and pays the three instalments from the delivery payment and her normal monthly sales. She needed a partner, not a lender, and no grant fits a commercial order at all.
Never borrow to cover losses

If the business is losing money every month, a loan does not fix it. It adds a repayment to a business that already cannot pay its costs. First find out why you are losing money (prices too low, waste, credit sales not collected), fix that, and only then consider growth funding.
What each funder wants to see

Each type of funder asks a different main question. A **grant maker** asks: does this create the change we exist to support, and will this person spend the money honestly and report on it? A **lender** asks: will this business repay on time, and if it does not, how do we recover our money? A **partner** asks: what do we gain, and can she deliver her side reliably? You will prepare all three answers in this course, but you should know which question you are answering before you write a single word.
Funding is not only money

Many of the most useful deals for small producers are not cash at all: a distributor who collects from your shop, a church or school that gives you a market, a larger maker who lets you use their NAFDAC-compliant production space at agreed hours. Keep these in mind whenever you think "I need money".
Start with one specific, costed need, never with "funding" in general.
Loans suit needs that earn money back quickly; grants suit needs with social value that do not repay directly.
A supplier, buyer or partner can sometimes provide the thing you need instead of cash.
Never borrow to cover ongoing losses.

Profit is not the same as cash

A business can show a profit and still fail to pay a loan. That happens when money is tied up in stock or in customers who have not paid yet. Lenders are repaid from **cash in the account on the repayment date**, so they look closely at the pattern in your bank statements: steady inflows, or big gaps?
Worked example: Funmi's readiness score
For example, Funmi bakes bread and meat pies in Abeokuta and wants about ₦600,000 (approximate) for a bigger oven. She runs the six-area check.
ID and registration: NIN and BVN yes, but no CAC certificate. Score 1.
Bank account: all sales go into her personal account mixed with family money. Score 0.
Records: she has a notebook of daily sales for eight months but no expenses. Score 1.
Track record: four years of trading, two schools buy weekly and would give references. Score 2.
Plan: she knows the oven cost and that it doubles her baking per batch, but has not worked out extra profit per month. Score 1.
Tax and compliance: no TIN; her packaged pies carry no NAFDAC number. Score 0. Total: 5 out of 12.

Funmi is not ready to apply yet. Her three priority gaps: register a business name with CAC and open a business account, start recording expenses so she can show monthly profit, and calculate the extra profit the oven would bring. She sets a 90-day target to raise her score to at least 10.
Three months of clean history beats none

If your sales currently go into a personal account, open a business account now and route every business payment through it, including POS and transfer sales. After three to six months you will have statements that speak for you. Funders often ask for six months or more, so the earlier you start, the sooner you qualify.
Choose your gaps wisely

You will probably find more gaps than you can close at once. Fix them in this order: first anything that makes you **ineligible** (no registration when the programme requires it), then anything that makes your numbers **unbelievable** (no records or bank history), and last anything that is simply nice to have. Two well-closed gaps are worth more than six half-started ones.
Funders judge you from evidence: ID, BVN, CAC, bank statements, records and track record.
Business bank statements are your strongest independent proof; start routing all sales through one account now.

Grants and support programmes

Grant money for small businesses in Nigeria usually comes through **programmes**, not open gifts. Examples include foundations such as the Tony Elumelu Foundation entrepreneurship programme, government agencies such as SMEDAN (the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria), state government empowerment schemes, international development projects, and corporate social responsibility programmes run by banks and large companies. Many include training, mentoring or equipment rather than only cash, and almost all open for a short window each year.

Because programmes change every year, never rely on a list someone forwarded on WhatsApp. Go to the organisation's **official website or verified social media page**, read the current call, and note the opening and closing dates yourself.
Partners
**Suppliers** who sell to you on credit or instalments.
**Buyers and distributors** who pay deposits, give purchase orders, or carry your product to new markets.
**Larger businesses** that share equipment, space or certification, or buy from small producers as part of their supply chain.
**Associations and NGOs** that pool members for bulk buying, training or group loans.

How to check that an offer is real
Find the organisation's official website yourself (do not click a link in a message) and confirm the programme is listed there.
For a bank or microfinance bank, check that it appears on the CBN's list of licensed institutions. For a loan app, check the FCCPC's published list of registered digital lenders.
Search the exact programme name plus the word "scam" or "fake" and read what comes up.
Ask: who is paying, and why? A real grant has a funder with a stated purpose and selection rules.
Never send money, your BVN, card details, OTP or PIN to anyone who contacts you about a grant.
The fee-before-grant trick

The most common scam goes like this: a message says you have been selected for a grant or a low-interest loan, but you must first pay a "processing", "registration", "insurance" or "release" fee. Real grant programmes do not ask winners to pay to receive their grant. Once you pay, the person disappears or asks for another fee. Delete the message, warn your group, and report it.
Worked example: Ifeoma checks two offers
For example, Ifeoma runs a small poultry farm near Owerri and needs feed and a few hundred day-old chicks before the festive season. In one week she receives two offers.
Offer 1: a WhatsApp broadcast says a "Federal Women Empowerment Grant" of ₦500,000 is open; she must pay ₦15,000 to a personal account to "activate" her slot.
She searches for the programme on the relevant ministry's official website and finds nothing. The payment goes to an individual, not an organisation. She deletes it.
Offer 2: her microfinance bank offers a 4-month poultry loan. She checks the bank on the CBN list of licensed microfinance banks and finds it there.
She asks for the full repayment schedule in writing, including every fee, before agreeing to anything.
Ifeoma avoids losing ₦15,000 to a scam and moves forward with a licensed lender whose terms she can check. In Module 2 you will learn to test whether a loan like hers can actually be repaid.

Applications fail for boring reasons far more often than for big ones: a missing document, a scanned certificate nobody can read, a form submitted an hour after the portal closed, a reference who never replied. The fix is to treat funding like any other business process, with a written workflow, a tracker and a ready pack of documents. In business language this is a **standard operating procedure (SOP)**: the same steps, done the same way, every time.
A person ticking items on a large checklist

The six stages of almost every application
**Confirm fit.** Read the full call or loan terms. Check eligibility line by line: location, sector, years trading, registration type, gender or age focus. If you fail any hard rule, stop.
**List requirements.** Copy every required document and question into your tracker. Note word limits and file size limits.
**Gather evidence.** Pull documents from your pack, request bank statements, ask referees early.
**Draft.** Write answers or fill the loan form using your need statement and numbers.
**Check.** Run the accuracy checks from Lesson 2 of this module. Ask one trusted person to read it.
**Submit and follow up.** Submit at least two days before the deadline, save the confirmation, and diary a follow-up date.

For a grant, Stage 4 is the biggest job, and the Institute's Proposal Writing course teaches each section in depth. For a loan, Stage 3 is usually the biggest, because lenders want statements, guarantor forms and sometimes a visit to your premises. For a partnership, Stages 1 and 4 become a conversation and a written agreement, covered in Module 3.

Every serious reviewer does the same thing first: compare. They compare the sales figure in your application with the money flowing through your bank statement. They compare the cost of the machine with the quotation you attached. They compare the number of customers you claim with the evidence you provide. When the numbers disagree and you have not explained why, trust drops sharply, and many applications are rejected at this point without the business ever being properly considered.

Worked example: Chioma's sales do not match
For example, Chioma sells fabrics in Onitsha. Her application says average monthly sales are about ₦1,800,000. Her six months of business statements show total inflows of ₦7,200,000.
Statement average: ₦7,200,000 ÷ 6 = ₦1,200,000 a month.
Gap: ₦1,800,000 minus ₦1,200,000 = ₦600,000 a month, a third of her claim.
She checks her records: about ₦500,000 a month is paid in cash and goes to an ajo contribution and stock purchases before reaching the bank.
The remaining ₦100,000 gap is because one month's figure in her draft was a festive peak, not an average.
She corrects her average to ₦1,700,000, based on her records, and adds a note: about ₦500,000 a month is cash, shown in her sales book, attached.

Chioma's claim is now backed by evidence and the difference is explained. A reviewer can see she is careful and honest, which is exactly what a lender is judging. She also starts banking all cash sales so the next statement tells the full story on its own.
Never inflate or invent

Adding figures, inventing customers, using someone else's photos, or editing a bank statement is dishonest, and changing a financial document can amount to forgery. It also usually fails: banks verify statements directly, credit bureaus reveal existing loans, and programmes visit winners. A smaller, true application beats a bigger false one every time.

Do the same with your **costs**. If you say the machine costs ₦650,000, attach a dated quotation for ₦650,000 from a real supplier, with their business name and phone number. If prices are rising quickly, say how old the quotation is and add a small, clearly labelled allowance for price change rather than quietly rounding up.
Point-by-point compliance

Read the call or loan form again and turn every requirement into a line on a checklist. Then tick each one only when you can point to the page or file that meets it. Watch especially for: word limits, required file types (PDF only?), the exact name format (as on your CAC certificate), signatures, dates on quotations, and questions with two parts where people answer only one.

Grant agreements and loan offers contain commitments that last long after the money arrives. Before you sign, find and write down each of these in plain words:

**Loans:** total amount repayable, every fee (management, insurance, processing), repayment dates, penalty for late payment, what happens to collateral or guarantors if you default, whether you can repay early without a charge.

**Grants:** what the money may and may not be spent on, reporting dates and format, whether you must keep receipts for a certain period, whether unspent money must be returned, use of your name and photos in their publicity.
**Both:** who to contact with problems, and what counts as breaking the agreement.
Ask questions in writing

If something in the terms is unclear, ask the officer by email or WhatsApp and keep the reply. A written answer protects you later if there is a disagreement, and a funder who refuses to explain their own terms is giving you useful information.

Calculate the total cost of a loan, including interest and fees
Compare a flat-rate quote with a reducing-balance quote

A loan is only good if your business can repay it on time **from its normal cash flow**, without borrowing again, selling assets or taking money meant for the family. This lesson gives you the arithmetic to check that yourself, instead of trusting the person selling the loan.
A woman working with a large calculator
Do the loan arithmetic yourself before anyone asks you to sign.
Step 1: the total cost

Ask every lender for the **full repayment schedule in writing**: each payment date, each amount, and every fee. Then add it up. Total cost = everything you will pay back minus the amount you actually receive. If a fee is taken from the loan before you receive it, you receive less money but still repay the full amount, which makes the loan more expensive than it looks.
Step 2: flat rate or reducing balance?

Many small business loans in Nigeria are quoted as a **monthly rate**. There are two very different ways to charge it. With a **flat rate**, interest is calculated on the full original amount for every month, even though you are repaying part of it each month. With a **reducing balance**, interest each month is calculated only on what you still owe. The same "3% a month" costs much more on a flat basis.

Worked example: two quotes for ₦500,000
For example, Grace sells frozen fish and chicken in Ibadan and wants ₦500,000 for six months to buy a second chest freezer and stock. Two lenders quote 3% a month.
Lender A, flat: interest = ₦500,000 x 3% x 6 = ₦90,000. Total repaid ₦590,000, or about ₦98,333 a month.
Lender B, reducing balance: the equal monthly payment works out to about ₦92,300 (a loan calculator app or spreadsheet gives this). Total repaid about ₦553,800, so interest is about ₦53,800.
Month 1 at Lender B: interest = ₦500,000 x 3% = ₦15,000, so about ₦77,300 of her ₦92,300 reduces the debt. By month 6, interest is only about ₦2,700.
Lender A also deducts a 2% management fee upfront: ₦10,000. She receives ₦490,000 but repays ₦590,000, a true cost of ₦100,000.
Lender B charges a 1% fee (₦5,000), so its true cost is about ₦58,800.
Both lenders said "3% a month", but Lender A costs Grace about ₦41,200 more. She chooses Lender B, and only after checking Step 3 below.
Let a spreadsheet do it

In Google Sheets, the formula =PMT(3%, 6, -500000) returns the equal monthly payment for a reducing-balance loan of ₦500,000 at 3% a month over six months (about ₦92,299). Change the numbers to test any quote in seconds.
Step 3: can your cash flow carry it?

Take the last six months from your records and bank statements. For each month, work out your **free cash**: money in, minus all business costs, minus what you take home for the family. That is the money genuinely available to repay a loan. A useful measure lenders use is the **debt service coverage ratio**: free cash divided by the loan repayment. Below 1 means you cannot pay from normal cash flow. Many careful lenders look for well above 1, so that one weak month does not cause a default. A cautious personal rule is to keep the repayment at no more than about two thirds of your average free cash.

Step 4: the bad-month test

Look at your worst month in the last year and ask: if that month came again, could I still repay? Grace's slowest month leaves her ₦7,300 short. She has three choices: hold back a **repayment reserve** of one month's payment from the loan or her savings before she starts; ask for a longer term so each payment is smaller; or borrow less. She also adds the extra profit the freezer will bring (she estimates about ₦40,000 a month from selling more stock without spoilage) but she does not count that money until it actually appears in her records.
Collateral, guarantors and your credit record

If you pledge equipment, land documents or a guarantor, you are risking those if you default. A guarantor can be asked to repay for you, which can damage a friendship or family. Late payments are also reported to credit bureaus and can block future loans. Only sign when the bad-month test passes.

A partnership is any arrangement where another business or organisation gives you something you need, and you give them something they value in return. Done well, it can do what a loan does without interest or collateral. Done badly, it can tie you to a buyer who pays late, or a partner who takes more than they give. The cash gap in a retail deal

Getting your product into a supermarket or a chain of shops feels like a win, and it can be. But big buyers often pay 30, 45 or 60 days after delivery, sometimes only for what has sold. During that time you have already paid for materials, packaging and transport. That waiting period is the **cash gap**, and you must fund it from somewhere.
Worked example: Ada's supermarket offer

For example, Ada makes chin-chin in Port Harcourt and sells about 400 packs a month at ₦1,500 each (approximate) through her WhatsApp customers. A local supermarket chain offers to stock her in three branches: 600 packs a month at a wholesale price of ₦1,200, paid 30 days after the end of each delivery month.
Her cost per pack (flour, sugar, oil, eggs, packaging, gas) is about ₦750.
Supermarket profit per pack: ₦1,200 minus ₦750 = ₦450. On 600 packs: ₦270,000 a month.
Cash she must spend each month to produce 600 packs: 600 x ₦750 = ₦450,000.
Payment arrives about 30 days after the end of the month, so she funds roughly two months of production before the first payment: about ₦900,000.
She has ₦300,000 saved. Gap: about ₦600,000.

She asks her flour and oil supplier for 30-day credit (they agree, covering about ₦250,000), and asks the supermarket to start with two branches (400 packs, ₦300,000 a month, about ₦600,000 for two months).

With supplier credit and a smaller start, Ada's cash need falls to about ₦350,000, close to her savings. She keeps her WhatsApp customers, proves reliable delivery for three months, then grows to the third branch. She solved most of the problem with partnerships, not a loan.
Proposing a partnership

Partners agree when they see clear value for themselves. Before you approach anyone, write down their likely interests: a supplier wants volume and reliable payment; a retailer wants products that sell, arrive on time, and carry proper labels and NAFDAC numbers where required; an NGO wants reach into a community it serves. Then make a short proposal: who you are, what you propose, what they gain, what you need from them, and the proof that you deliver.

Put it in writing

A **memorandum of understanding (MoU)** or simple agreement does not need a lawyer for small deals, though a lawyer is wise for anything involving large sums, property or shares in your business. It should cover, in plain words:
The names of both parties, exactly as registered.
What each side will provide, in quantities, standards and dates.
Prices, payment terms and what happens if payment is late.
Who owns what: equipment, brand names, recipes, customer lists.
How long the agreement lasts, how to end it, and the notice period.
How disagreements will be handled, and signatures and dates of both sides.
Protect your recipe and your brand

Do not hand over your recipe, supplier list or customer list to a partner unless the agreement clearly says what they may do with it. Be very careful with anyone who asks for a share of your business in return for help: that is a permanent change of ownership, and it needs proper legal advice and registration with CAC.

Set up a spending plan and a separate record for funded money

Getting the money is half the job. How you use it decides whether you will ever be funded again. Funders and lenders talk to each other, and programmes often ask applicants about past grants and loans. A well-used, well-reported first grant or loan is the strongest evidence you can bring to the next one.
A person sending a report with charts to an investor
A short, honest update to your funder builds the track record that unlocks the next round.
Ring-fence the money

Keep funded money separate from day-to-day takings. The cleanest way is a separate business sub-account or a second business account used only for the grant or loan. Pay suppliers directly from it by transfer, so each payment shows on the statement. Collect a receipt or invoice for every payment, photograph it the same day, and store it in a folder named after the grant or loan.

If you must pay a small market trader in cash, ask for a handwritten receipt with the date, item, amount, their name and phone number, and photograph the item. Keep cash payments rare, because they are the hardest to prove later.
Budget against actual
Write your spending plan from your application as a table, then add a column for what you actually spent and a column for the difference. Update it every week while you are spending.
Worked example: Bukola's equipment grant
For example, Bukola runs a small catering business in Ilorin and receives a ₦1,000,000 grant for a commercial gas cooker, a chest freezer and food hygiene training for herself and two helpers.
Planned: cooker ₦450,000, freezer ₦380,000, training ₦120,000, delivery and installation ₦50,000. Total ₦1,000,000.
Actual: cooker ₦470,000 (price rose between quote and purchase), freezer ₦365,000, training ₦120,000, delivery ₦45,000.
Differences: cooker +₦20,000, freezer −₦15,000, delivery −₦5,000. The savings covered the cooker increase exactly.
She checks her grant agreement: moving money between lines is allowed up to 10% of a line without permission. ₦20,000 is about 4% of the cooker line, so she simply explains it in her report.

Bukola's report shows every naira, with receipts, and a one-line explanation of the price change. Had the change been larger than her agreement allowed, she would have written to the funder for approval before buying.

Writing a progress report

Use the funder's format if they provide one. If not, keep it to one or two pages with these parts: what you planned, what you did, what it cost against budget, the results so far in numbers, problems and how you handled them, and what comes next. Include photos of the equipment in use or the training taking place. Report bad news early and plainly: a funder who hears about a delay from you, with a plan to fix it, reacts very differently from one who discovers it.
Results in numbers: "Weekly output rose from 60 to 110 meals in month two" beats "business has improved".
Compare with your starting point (the baseline) from your application.

Funded growth that outruns your ability to train people leads to poor quality, waste and unhappy customers, which then shows up in your report.

Keep the pack in two forms: your private digital Funding Pack folder, and a printed, labelled file for meetings with bank officers or partners. Update the financial section every month. A pack that was ready six months ago but has old statements is no longer ready.
A one-page funding proposal

Many conversations start with a single page, so write one. It should state who you are and how long you have traded; your current monthly sales and profit (from records); the exact need and its cost; how it will be funded (amount from you, from the funder or lender, from a partner); the result in numbers and by when; and, for a loan, how repayments will be met, showing your free cash.
Worked example: Ruth's final gap check and 90-day plan

For example, Ruth runs a small fruit juice and zobo business in Jos. She started this course with a readiness score of 6 out of 12. Her need: a commercial juice extractor and a chest freezer, about ₦850,000 (approximate) together, to supply two hotels that have asked for daily deliveries.
Gap check now: CAC done, business account opened four months ago, records complete for six months, loan check done. New score: 10 out of 12.
Remaining gaps: only four months of business statements (her shortlisted lender asks for six), and her zobo label has no NAFDAC number, which the hotels' purchasing officer has asked about.
Funding mix: ₦200,000 of her own savings, a written 50% deposit from one hotel on its first monthly order (about ₦150,000), and a microfinance bank loan of ₦500,000.

Loan check: at the quoted 2% a month on a reducing balance over 12 months, =PMT(2%, 12, -500000) gives about ₦47,280 a month. Her worst recent month had ₦60,000 free cash; average is ₦110,000. The bad-month test passes.
Days 1 to 30: start the NAFDAC process for zobo (it takes time, so she begins at once), get the hotel deposit agreement in writing.
Days 31 to 60: sixth month of statements arrives; submit the loan application with the full pack.
Days 61 to 90: buy equipment, train her helper, begin hotel deliveries, send each hotel a monthly delivery summary.
Ruth's plan names a real lender, a real partner and dated actions. She knows exactly which two gaps stand between her and funding, and how long each will take.

Before you call the pack finished, hand it to one trusted person who knows business, such as a cooperative secretary, an accountant friend or a mentor, and ask them to read it as if they were the lender. Their questions show you exactly where a real reviewer would hesitate. Fix those points, then date the pack so you know when it next needs updating.
From one round to the next

Each successful round builds the next. A small loan repaid on time strengthens your credit record for a larger one. A grant used well and reported honestly becomes evidence for the next programme. A partner who has seen three months of reliable delivery is more likely to extend credit or a bigger order. Keep a short **funding history** page in your pack: what you received, from whom, for what, and the result.
Say no when it is right

Part of being funding-ready is declining offers that do not fit: a loan that fails the bad-month test, a grant whose rules would pull you away from your business, or a partner whose terms would take your brand. Every no that protects your business is a good decision.

Why this matters
Four places growth money comes from
Your own money: nothing to repay
Grant: no repayment, strict rules
Loan: repaid with interest and fees
Partnership: someone supplies what you need
Growth money can come from four places, and each has a price. Your own savings or ajo payout costs nothing to repay, but it may be your safety buffer.
A grant needs no repayment, but competition is heavy and the spending rules are strict.
A loan is repaid with interest and fees on a fixed schedule. Miss payments, and you can lose collateral or your credit record.

A partnership is when a supplier, buyer or bigger business gives you credit, equipment, space or buyers. The goal of this course is to get what you need without putting your business or your home at risk.
Start with the need
Weak need versus strong need
Weak
"I need money to grow"
No cost, no result
Strong
Two machines, about ₦650,000
40 uniforms a week instead of 15
Accept two school contracts
The most common mistake is looking for funding first and deciding what to do with it later. I need money to grow my fashion business tells a funder nothing.

A strong need says what you will buy, what it costs, and the result in numbers. For example: two industrial machines, about 650,000 naira, so I can sew 40 uniforms a week instead of 15 and accept the two school contracts I turned down.
Choose the route
Will this need bring money back?
How soon, and how much?
Can someone supply it instead of cash?
Question one. Will this need bring money back? New stock or a machine for orders you already have usually will. A fancy signboard may not.
Question two. How soon, and how much? Loan repayments usually start within a month, so a slow return is a danger sign for borrowing.
Question three. Could a supplier give you 30 days to pay, a buyer pay a deposit, or a cooperative share a machine? Then you may not need cash at all.
And if the business is losing money every month, a loan does not fix it. Find out why first: prices too low, waste, or credit sales not collected.

Many people pretend to offer funding. Find the organisation's official website yourself, never through a link in a message. Check banks on the CBN list and loan apps on the FCCPC list.
Search the programme name plus the word scam. And ask: who is paying, and why?

Real grant programmes do not ask winners to pay a fee. For example, Ifeoma was told to pay 15,000 naira to a personal account to activate a 500,000 naira grant. She found nothing on the official website and deleted it.
Never send money, your BVN, card details, OTP or PIN to anyone about a grant.

Why this matters
Most applications fail for boring reasons
Missing documents and late submissions
Numbers that do not match
Loans that cost more than they look
Repayments that one bad month breaks
Applications fail for boring reasons far more often than big ones: a missing document, a form submitted an hour after the portal closed.
Or numbers that disagree, with no explanation. Reviewers always compare.
And a loan is only good if your business can repay it from normal cash flow, without borrowing again or taking money meant for the family. Today you learn to check all of this yourself.
Your workflow
Six stages of every application
Confirm fit: check every eligibility rule
List every requirement in your tracker
Gather evidence from your Funding Pack
Draft using your need statement
Check figures; a trusted person reads it
Submit early, save proof, diary follow-up
Submit at least two days before the deadline.
Treat applying like any business process. Stage one, confirm fit. Check eligibility line by line. If you fail a hard rule, stop.
Stage two, copy every requirement into one tracker, with word and file size limits.
Stage three, gather evidence from a private Funding Pack folder of clearly named scans. Never post these documents in group chats.
Stage four, draft your answers from your need statement and numbers.
Stage five, check every figure, and ask one trusted person to read it.
Stage six, submit early, save the confirmation, and diary a follow-up date. For example, Amina in Kano planned backwards from a 21 March deadline and submitted on 18 March, three days early.

Put three sources side by side: what you wrote, your records, and your bank statements. They should tell the same story.
Chioma's application says her sales are about 1,800,000 naira a month.
Her six months of statements show 7,200,000 naira in total, which is 1,200,000 a month. A gap of 600,000.
Her records explain most of it. About 500,000 naira a month is paid in cash and spent on ajo and stock before it reaches the bank. The rest came from using a festive month as an average.

Never inflate figures or edit a statement. It is dishonest, changing a financial document can be forgery, and banks check.

For example, Grace sells frozen fish and chicken in Ibadan. She wants 500,000 naira for six months, and two lenders both quote 3% a month. Always ask for the full repayment schedule in writing.
Lender A charges a flat rate: interest on the full 500,000 every month. That is 90,000 naira. It also takes a 2% fee upfront, so she receives 490,000 but repays 590,000. A true cost of 100,000 naira.
Lender B uses a reducing balance: interest only on what she still owes. That is about 53,800 naira, plus a 1% fee. A true cost of about 58,800 naira.
Both said 3% a month, but Lender A costs her about 41,200 naira more.
The bad-month test
Can her cash flow carry ₦92,300?
Free cash about ₦150,000. After the repayment, ₦57,700 is left.
Free cash about ₦85,000. After the repayment, she is ₦7,300 short.
Hold back a reserve of one month's payment, ask for a longer term, or borrow less.
Now the most important test. Free cash is money in, minus business costs, minus what you take home for the family. Lender B's payment is about 92,300 naira a month.
In an average month Grace has about 150,000 naira free, so 57,700 is left.
But in her slowest month she had only about 85,000 naira. She would be 7,300 short.
So before signing, she holds back a reserve of one month's payment, or asks for a longer term, or borrows less. And she does not count the freezer's extra profit until it shows in her records.

Total amount repayable
Every fee
Repayment dates
Penalty for late payment

Before you sign any loan, write down the total repayable, every fee, the dates, and the late penalty.
Know what happens to collateral or a guarantor if you default. A guarantor can be asked to repay for you, and late payments go to credit bureaus. Only sign when the bad-month test passes.

A good partnership can do what a loan does, without interest or collateral. But selling to big buyers on credit creates a waiting period you must fund.
Getting money is half the job. How you use and report it decides whether you are ever funded again.
The cash gap
Ada's supermarket offer
For example, Ada makes chin-chin in Port Harcourt. A supermarket offers 600 packs a month at ₦1,200.
Profit on 600 packs a month
Cost to produce 600 packs
Two months before first payment

Ada makes chin-chin in Port Harcourt. A supermarket chain offers to take 600 packs a month at 1,200 naira each, paid 30 days after the end of each delivery month.
Each pack costs her about 750 naira, so she makes 450 naira a pack, or 270,000 naira a month.
But she must spend 450,000 naira a month to produce them.
Because payment comes late, she funds about two months first: 900,000 naira. That waiting period is the cash gap.

She has only 300,000 saved. So her supplier gives 30-day credit, and she starts with two branches instead of three. Her cash need falls to about 350,000 naira, close to her savings. Partnerships, not a loan.

Both names, exactly as registered

Prices, payment terms, late payment

Write every partnership down. Name both sides, what each provides and when, prices and payment terms, who owns what, how long it lasts and how to end it, and signatures with dates.
Never hand over your recipe or customer list without clear terms. And anyone asking for a share of your business needs proper legal advice and registration with CAC.
Protect the money
Ring-fence funded money
Use a separate account for the grant or loan
Pay suppliers by transfer
Keep invoice, receipt and delivery photo
Compare plan and actual every week
Report results and problems early
Keep funded money apart from daily takings.
Keep grant or loan money in a separate account, used only for that purpose.
Pay suppliers by transfer, so every payment shows on the statement. Keep cash payments rare.
For every payment, keep the invoice, the transfer receipt, and a delivery note or photo. Photograph receipts the same day.
Compare your plan with what you actually spent every week. And report problems early and plainly. A funder who hears about a delay from you reacts very differently from one who discovers it.

Bukola runs a catering business in Ilorin. She receives a 1,000,000 naira grant for a gas cooker, a chest freezer and hygiene training.

Funded growth often brings equipment and new hands. If equipment uses gas, electricity or heat, have a qualified person install it.

Train on safety first, and show every worker how to switch off the gas and power. Show, then watch, then check their work daily for the first two weeks. An accident hurts people first, and it also ends funding relationships.
